watersheds-s2.title: Rain and runoff in two small watersheds

table.caption: The same storm (30 mm of rain) over two watersheds of 4 km² each (invented data for practice)
cols: Share of the rain that ran off (%)
Sediment in the stream after the storm (mg/L)

options: The land that drains into one stream, river or lake
A layer of rock and sediment that stores groundwater
A dam built to hold water for a city
The point where a river reaches the ocean

why.correct: A watershed (drainage basin) is an area of land: every drop that falls inside its divide runs off or flows underground toward the same body of water.
options: Right: a watershed is the land that drains to one body of water.
Water stored underground in rock and sediment is an aquifer, not a watershed.
A dam holds water, but a watershed is the land around it that drains in.
That is the river's mouth; the watershed is all the land upstream that drains to it.

items.q: What separates one watershed from the next?
options: A divide: a ridge or high ground
A river: the main channel in the valley
A dam: a wall across the valley
A water table: the top of the groundwater

why.correct: Water flows downhill, so the high ground between two valleys decides which way rain runs. That ridge line is the divide.
options: Right: a divide of high ground separates watersheds.
The main river runs through the middle of a watershed, not along its edge.
A dam sits across a river inside one watershed.
The water table is underground; watersheds are set by the land surface.

items.q: A town takes its drinking water from a river. A factory 80 km upstream, in the same watershed, starts dumping waste into a small stream that feeds the river. Why should the town be concerned?
options: Streams in a watershed flow down to the same river
The waste will soak into the aquifer under the factory
Waste in a small stream evaporates before reaching a river
Streams flow toward their sources, so waste stays upstream

why.correct: Every stream in a watershed drains toward the same outlet. What enters a small stream upstream can be carried downstream to the town.
options: Right: tributaries carry pollutants downstream to the main river.
The waste is dumped into a stream, which flows on to the river.
Water evaporates, but most dissolved pollutants stay in the water.
Rivers flow downhill, away from their sources, toward the town.

items.q: Two watersheds get the same storm. One is mostly forest and the other is mostly pavement and rooftops. Which statement best describes the difference?
options: The paved one has more runoff and higher floods
The forested one has more runoff, as trees block infiltration
Both have equal runoff, because they got the same rain
The paved one has more infiltration into groundwater

why.correct: Forest soils, leaf litter and roots let rain soak in and slow its flow. Pavement and roofs shed water, so more runs off and reaches streams quickly, raising flood peaks.
options: Right: pavement turns rain into fast runoff.
Tree roots and leaf litter help water soak in, not block it.
The same rain can produce very different runoff depending on land cover.
Pavement blocks infiltration, so less water recharges groundwater.

items.q: Which features of a watershed increase the runoff and erosion that follow a storm? Select all that apply.
options: Steep slopes
Bare or paved ground
Deep, sandy soil
Thick forest cover

why.correct: Water runs off steep, bare or paved ground quickly. Permeable soil and plant cover let water soak in and hold soil in place.
options: Right: steep slopes speed up runoff and erosion.
Right: bare or paved ground lets less water soak in.
Sandy soil is permeable, so more water soaks in and less runs off.
Forest cover slows water and lets it soak in.

items.q: A news report says a city "draws its water from the Ogallala Aquifer, in the Platte River watershed." What is the difference between the two terms?
options: A watershed is land draining to a river; an aquifer stores water underground
An aquifer is land draining to a river; a watershed stores water underground
Both mean the same thing: an area of land that collects rainwater
The aquifer is the river's main channel; the watershed is the tributaries

why.correct: A watershed is defined by the land surface and where it drains. An aquifer is underground: a layer of sand, gravel or rock whose pores hold groundwater. One region can contain both.
options: Right: a watershed is surface land; an aquifer is underground water storage.
This swaps the two definitions.
They are different: one is land surface, the other underground storage.
An aquifer is underground, not a river channel.

items.q: In the map view, rain falls just outside the dashed divide of watershed A, on the side toward watershed B. Where does that water go?
options: Into the streams of watershed B
Into the lake at the outlet of watershed A
Straight into the aquifer under watershed A
It stays where it fell

why.correct: The divide is the high ground. Rain on the far side runs downhill away from watershed A and into watershed B.
options: Right: water on the far side of the divide drains to watershed B.
Only rain inside the divide drains to watershed A's lake.
Water first runs downhill on the surface; the divide decides which watershed it joins.
Water on a slope moves downhill as runoff or infiltration.

items.q: In the cut-away view, what happens to rain that does not run off into the stream?
options: It soaks in and can recharge the aquifer
It flows over the divide into the next watershed
It is held on the land surface as runoff
It moves up into the stream through the bedrock

why.correct: Water that soaks in moves down through soil until it reaches the water table, refilling the aquifer.
options: Right: infiltration recharges the aquifer.
Water soaking in moves down, not over the divide.
Runoff is water moving over the surface, the water that did not soak in.
The rock at the bottom of the diagram does not let water pass.

items.q: A county wants to protect both its stream and its well water. Using the diagram, why should it protect land across the whole watershed, not just the stream banks?
options: Water from across the watershed reaches the stream and the aquifer
Land along the banks is the main source of the stream's water
The aquifer is refilled by the ocean, not by the land above it
Protecting the banks would keep rain from reaching the stream

why.correct: Rain falling anywhere inside the divide either runs off to the stream or soaks down toward the aquifer, carrying whatever is on the land with it.
options: Right: the whole watershed feeds both the stream and the aquifer.
All the land inside the divide drains to the stream, not just the banks.
The diagram shows infiltration from the land surface recharging the aquifer.
Rain still reaches the stream as runoff from the rest of the watershed.

items.q: Which comparison does the table support?
options: More runoff went with more sediment
More runoff went with less sediment
The forest had more runoff than the paved land
Both streams carried similar sediment

why.correct: South Creek had 55% runoff and 640 mg/L of sediment; North Creek had 10% runoff and 20 mg/L.
options: Right: the watershed with more runoff carried far more sediment.
The data show the opposite: more runoff, more sediment.
The forested North Creek had 10% runoff, the least.
640 mg/L is 32 times 20 mg/L.

items.q: The storm dropped 30 mm (0.03 m) of rain on South Creek's 4 km² (4,000,000 m²), and 55% ran off. Write the setup for the volume of runoff in cubic meters, with units, then the answer.

why.correct: $0.03\,\text{m} \times 4{,}000{,}000\,\text{m}^{2} \times 0.55 = 66{,}000\,\text{m}^{3}$. Meters times square meters gives cubic meters.

mistakes.why: This is all the rain that fell. Only 55% ran off: multiply by 0.55.
30 mm is 0.03 m, not 30 m. Convert before you multiply so the units match.
That is all the rain that fell (0.03 × 4,000,000). Take 55% of it.
A factor of 1,000: 30 mm is 0.03 m, not 30 m.

items.q: Use the table. How many times more runoff, as a share of the rain, did South Creek have than North Creek?

mistakes.why: That is the difference in percentage points. "How many times" means divide: 55 ÷ 10.
Put the larger share on top: 55 ÷ 10.

items.q: A student concludes, "Paving causes more sediment in streams." Why is this conclusion not fully supported by the data in the table?
options: South Creek differs in both land cover and slope
The two watersheds got different amounts of rain
Sediment was not measured in South Creek
The two watersheds are of different sizes

why.correct: South Creek is both paved or plowed and steep. Steep slopes also raise runoff and erosion, so the data cannot separate the two causes.
options: Right: two variables differ, so they are confounded.
The caption says both got the same 30 mm storm.
The table gives sediment for both creeks.
Both watersheds are 4 km².

items.q: Propose a way to reduce sediment entering a stream from a steep, plowed field next to it, and say how it works.

why.correct: A solution fits the scenario (a field next to a stream) and says how it works: plants slow the water and roots hold the soil.

specific.frame: Plant ___ along the stream, which ___, so ___.

action.label: Action
options: a strip of grass and trees
a row of fertilized crops
nothing, leaving the bank bare

why.1: More plowed, fertilized crops leave soil exposed and add nutrients to runoff.

how.label: How it works
options: slows runoff and lets roots hold the soil
speeds runoff into the stream
raises the water temperature

why.2: Warmer water does not stop sediment.

result.label: Result
options: less sediment reaches the stream
more sediment reaches the stream
the watershed gets larger

why.1: The goal is to reduce sediment.
why.2: Plants do not change the area of the watershed.

specific.model: Plant a strip of grass and trees along the stream, which slows runoff so sediment settles out, and the roots hold the bank soil, which reduces the sediment that reaches the stream.

items.q: Mill Creek flows into the Ohio River, which flows into the Mississippi River. How is the Mill Creek watershed related to the Mississippi River watershed?
options: It is a small part of the Mississippi watershed
It is a separate watershed with its own outlet to the sea
It is larger than the Mississippi watershed
It is the aquifer that feeds the Mississippi

why.correct: Watersheds nest. Everything that drains to Mill Creek then drains to the Ohio and then the Mississippi, so the creek's watershed lies inside the larger ones.
options: Right: small watersheds nest inside larger ones.
Mill Creek's water reaches the sea through the Mississippi, so it is not separate.
A tributary's watershed is smaller than the river basin it drains into.
A watershed is surface land, not an aquifer.
